passage: Before: In the morning, Tanu, two, sat on her grandfather's lap while he read the newspaper. During: When she bumped her head at noon, her aunt was nearest and picked her up, and Tanu stopped crying against her shoulder. Her cousin made faces until she laughed. After: By evening, she fell asleep on her grandmother's bed while her mother cooked. Nobody worried. In this big house, many arms felt like home.

qa.q: Whose lap did Tanu sit on in the morning?
qa.a: Her grandfather's lap.

qa.q: Why did Tanu stop crying with her aunt?
qa.a: Her aunt is one of many familiar faces she trusts, so any of them can soothe her. 🙂

qa.q: What is a strength of having many caregivers?
qa.a: Tanu feels safe with several people, so comfort is always nearby.

qa.q: How might Tanu's mother feel as she cooks?
qa.a: Relaxed, knowing others in the house are caring for Tanu.

grounding: It shows a toddler in a joint household soothed and cared for by many familiar people.

passage: In a big old house in Lucknow, two-year-old Ayaan lived with his parents, grandparents, two aunts and three cousins. When he fell off the steps, his uncle was nearest. He scooped Ayaan up and rocked him. Ayaan cried a little, then rested his head on his uncle's chest. Soon his grandmother called him for mango slices, and he toddled over, smiling. His mother, at work, did not worry.

qa.q: Who was nearest when Ayaan fell off the steps?
qa.a: His uncle.

qa.q: Why did Ayaan calm down so quickly with his uncle?
qa.a: His uncle is a familiar, trusted face, so his comfort worked just as well.

qa.q: What does this show about joint families?
qa.a: Attachment spreads across many people, so a child can be soothed by whoever is nearby.

qa.q: How might his mother feel knowing this?
qa.a: Reassured that Ayaan is cared for even while she is at work. 🙂

grounding: It illustrates a toddler in a joint family comforted by whoever is nearest.

passage: "Who's crying?" called Dadi from the kitchen. "It's Mini," said her cousin Rahul, eight. "She dropped her doll." "I'll get her," said Chachi, putting down the vegetables. She lifted Mini, two, and wiped her face. "Where's Mama?" Mini sniffled. "At the market. Chachi is here." Mini leaned on her shoulder and stopped crying. Then Dada called, "Mini, come see the parrot!" and she wriggled down and ran to him.

qa.q: What did Mini drop?
qa.a: Her doll.

qa.q: Why did Mini stop crying with Chachi?
qa.a: Chachi is one of many familiar people she trusts, so her comfort felt safe.

qa.q: What does this show about joint households?
qa.a: Many adults share care, so a child feels secure with several caregivers.

qa.q: How might Rahul experience helping with Mini?
qa.a: He likely feels part of caring for his little cousin. 🙂

grounding: It shows a toddler in a joint family soothed by many caregivers.

passage: "I'm just getting water, Kabir," said Mama, standing up. Kabir, two, wailed and grabbed her leg. "Mama, no!" Papa knelt. "I'm here, buddy." Kabir kept crying, reaching for the kitchen door. "She'll be right back." Mama returned with the glass. Kabir clung to her, hiccupping. "Only a minute," she laughed softly. The flat was quiet again.

qa.q: What did Mama go to get?
qa.a: Water.

qa.q: Why did Kabir cry so hard when Mama left for a minute?
qa.a: He is closely tied to his two parents, so even a short absence feels big.

qa.q: What could help Kabir feel safer?
qa.a: Telling him clearly where Mama is going and coming back quickly, as she did. 🙂

qa.q: How might Papa feel when Kabir kept crying?
qa.a: A bit helpless, but patient.

grounding: It shows a toddler in a nuclear home strongly attached to his parents and upset when one leaves.

passage: Daycare note. Zoya, two, lives with just her mum and dad. At drop-off she cries hard and clings to her mother for several minutes. With us she is quieter at first and looks at the door often. When her father comes to pick her up, she runs to him with a huge smile. I think her bond with her parents is very deep. We will keep her mornings calm and give her one special teacher to stay with.

qa.q: Who does Zoya live with?
qa.a: Just her mum and dad.

qa.q: Why does Zoya cry hard at drop-off?
qa.a: Her bond is deep but centred on her two parents, so leaving them feels hard.

qa.q: What is good about the daycare's plan?
qa.a: Giving her one special teacher helps her build a new close bond more easily. 👍

qa.q: How might her father feel when she runs to him?
qa.a: Happy and loved.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler in a nuclear family with deep, narrow bonds, distressed at separation.

passage: In a small town house near Mysuru, two-year-old Anu lived alone with her parents. When her mother stepped out to the shop next door, Anu stood at the window and cried loudly. Her father picked her up and showed her the street. "Amma is coming," he said. She kept pointing at the door. When her mother returned, Anu reached out and buried her face in her neck. Their days were quiet and close.

qa.q: Where did Anu's mother go?
qa.a: To the shop next door.

qa.q: Why did Anu cry at the window?
qa.a: She is closely tied to her few caregivers, so her mother leaving felt upsetting even with her father there.

qa.q: What did her father do well?
qa.a: He stayed calm, held her and reassured her that Amma was coming. 🙂

qa.q: How might her mother feel when Anu buried her face in her neck?
qa.a: Loved, and perhaps a little worried about leaving her.

grounding: It shows a toddler in a nuclear home with close bonds and sharp distress when a parent leaves.

passage: At the community centre summer camp, five-year-old Rohan, who lived with six cousins at home, handed his crayons to a new boy without being asked. When the new boy grabbed Rohan's snack, Rohan shouted, "Hey!" and pushed him. A minute later, Rohan broke his biscuit in half and gave him a piece. The camp leader smiled. The new boy, an only child, looked confused about how quickly they were friends again.

qa.q: How many cousins does Rohan live with?
qa.a: Six cousins.

qa.q: Why did Rohan share so quickly after the push?
qa.a: Living with many cousins, he is used to fighting and making up fast. 🙂

qa.q: What could the camp leader encourage?
qa.a: Rohan's easy sharing while helping him use words instead of pushing.

qa.q: How might the new boy experience Rohan?
qa.a: Confused but happy, as he is not used to making up so fast.

grounding: It shows a child from a big family sharing freely and fighting and making up quickly.

passage: I'm Meera's older cousin. In our house there are seven of us kids. Meera, five, shares her bed with two cousins, and nobody asks her. She hands out biscuits to everyone before eating one herself. Yesterday she fought with Arjun over the swing and they both cried. Ten minutes later they were sharing a mango. I don't think she even knows what privacy means yet. She just knows we're all together.

qa.q: How many kids are in the house?
qa.a: Seven.

qa.q: What does Meera handing out biscuits first suggest?
qa.a: She takes sharing for granted as part of belonging in a big family.

qa.q: What might Meera need later as she grows?
qa.a: Some space of her own, as privacy becomes more important. 🙂

qa.q: How does the cousin see Meera's quick fights and make-ups?
qa.a: As normal in their big family, where belonging is taken for granted.

grounding: It illustrates a child among cousins sharing everything and fighting and making up quickly.

passage: Before: In summer, Aarav, five, moved into his grandparents' house with four cousins. At first he cried when they used his toys. During: By autumn, he shared his bed with cousin Tia and passed rotis around at dinner without being told. He fought with Karan over the TV, then made up in minutes. After: By winter, when his friend asked if he had his own room, Aarav looked puzzled. "Why would I?"

qa.q: How many cousins did Aarav live with?
qa.a: Four cousins.

qa.q: Why did Aarav look puzzled at the question about his own room?
qa.a: In a shared home, belonging is taken for granted, and privacy is not yet a need. 😊

qa.q: What helped Aarav adjust?
qa.a: Living closely with cousins taught him to share and make up quickly.

qa.q: How might his friend see Aarav's answer?
qa.a: The friend might find it surprising if they have their own room.

grounding: It shows a child learning to share space and make up quickly in a joint household.

passage: Before: When her grandchildren moved in, Kamala Paati, seventy, prayed alone each morning. During: Within weeks, nine-year-old Shruti and seven-year-old Vikram sat beside her, copying her words and hand movements. At night, they begged for her stories. Vikram started using her old sayings, like "Slow water cuts stone." After: Paati noticed and felt a warmth she had not felt in years. Her son said, "They'd never learn this in our flat in Delhi." She smiled. "They learn what they see."

qa.q: What saying did Vikram start using?
qa.a: Slow water cuts stone.

qa.q: How did Paati feel when she noticed the children copying her?
qa.a: Warm and proud, feeling her role had meaning again. 😊

qa.q: What might a nuclear family do to pass on such traditions?
qa.a: Deliberately make time for grandparents' stories and prayers, through visits or calls.

qa.q: How might Shruti experience these mornings?
qa.a: As a special time of closeness and learning with her grandmother.

grounding: It shows a grandmother noticing grandchildren copy her prayers and sayings, giving her role meaning.

passage: Let me tell you something, Aditi. When you and your brother were small and we lived together, I never thought much about it. But one day I heard you saying my old prayer while playing. Then your brother used my saying about patience at school. My heart filled. I realised I was teaching you just by living with you. Your parents were busy with work. I had time. When you have children, find ways for them to be near their elders.

qa.q: What did the grandparent hear Aditi saying while playing?
qa.a: The grandparent's old prayer.

qa.q: How did the grandparent feel hearing it?
qa.a: Their heart filled with joy, realising they were teaching simply by living together. ❤️

qa.q: What advice does the grandparent give?
qa.a: When Aditi has children, to find ways for them to be near their elders.

qa.q: How might Aditi feel hearing this?
qa.a: Touched, and more aware of what her grandparent gave her.

grounding: It illustrates a grandparent noticing grandchildren absorbing prayers and sayings through daily contact.

passage: With the power cut on a hot evening, there was no TV and no fan. Grandma Rosa, in her small house in Goa, lit a lamp and began telling stories to her grandchildren, Leo, ten, and Maria, eight. Maria repeated her Konkani phrases, laughing. Leo asked about the old village. Rosa watched them and felt useful in a way she hadn't since her husband died. Their parents, who lived in the city flat, rarely heard these stories. Rosa decided to tell one every visit.

qa.q: What did Grandma Rosa light?
qa.a: A lamp.

qa.q: How did Rosa feel watching the children?
qa.a: Useful and meaningful, a feeling she hadn't had since her husband died. 🙂

qa.q: What did Rosa decide to do?
qa.a: Tell a story every visit so the children keep learning.

qa.q: How might Maria experience learning Konkani phrases?
qa.a: As fun and a way to feel close to her grandmother.

grounding: It shows a grandmother noticing grandchildren learning her language and stories, giving her role meaning.

passage: In a flat in Dubai, five-year-old Aarav met his father's friend. "Say hello to Ravi uncle," said his mother. "Hello Ravi," said Aarav. His mother whispered, "Ravi uncle." Aarav repeated, "Ravi uncle." The man laughed warmly and ruffled his hair. Later, Aarav called the older girl next door "Sana didi" without being told. She smiled and gave him a sweet. Aarav didn't know why, but saying didi seemed to make people happy.

qa.q: What did Aarav call the older girl next door?
qa.a: Sana didi.

qa.q: Why did Aarav keep using titles?
qa.a: He noticed people smiled when he used them, even though he did not yet understand their meaning. 😊

qa.q: How could his parents help him understand?
qa.a: Explain that these words show warmth and respect for older people.

qa.q: How might Ravi uncle feel being called uncle?
qa.a: Warm and pleased, shown by his laugh.

grounding: It shows a child copying honorifics like uncle and didi before understanding their warmth and rank.

passage: At the KG classroom, the teacher, Mrs. Mehta, taught the children to say "Good morning, Ma'am" and to call the helpers "Didi" and "Bhaiya". Five-year-old Riya kept calling the helper "Shanti" by name. The teacher gently said, "Shanti didi." Riya repeated it, puzzled. Later, when Shanti didi helped her tie her shoe, Riya said, "Thank you, Shanti didi," and hugged her. Shanti didi beamed.

qa.q: What did Riya keep calling the helper at first?
qa.a: Shanti, by name.

qa.q: Why was Riya puzzled when corrected?
qa.a: She was just copying the sound and did not yet understand why the title mattered.

qa.q: What did the teacher do well?
qa.a: She corrected Riya gently, letting her learn by repeating.

qa.q: How did Shanti didi feel when Riya thanked her with the title?
qa.a: Happy; she beamed. 🙂

grounding: It illustrates a child learning to use honorifics by copying before understanding their warmth.

passage: I'm Kabir's aunt. At the family wedding, Kabir, four, was told to say "namaste ji" to all the elders. He said "nam-ji" to everyone, quickly, like a game. The elders laughed and blessed him. When he met his cousin, he said "Bhaiya!" and jumped on him. I don't think he knows what the words mean yet. But he knows they make people smile, and he says them with warmth.

qa.q: What did Kabir say to all the elders?
qa.a: Nam-ji, quickly, like a game.

qa.q: What does Kabir seem to understand about the titles?
qa.a: That they make people smile, though he does not yet know what they mean. 🤔

qa.q: How could the family help him learn more?
qa.a: Explain simply that the words show love and respect for elders.

qa.q: How did the elders respond to Kabir?
qa.a: They laughed and blessed him.

grounding: It shows a child copying honorific sounds with warmth before understanding their meaning.

passage: Counsellor's note, Class 5. Arjun, ten, came in upset. His uncle had said he should not argue about which shop sells cheaper rice, even though Arjun had checked the prices. "Respect your elders," his uncle said. Arjun told me, "But I was right. Why is respect about being quiet?" We talked about how respect can mean speaking politely and listening, not being afraid. I suggested he could say, "Uncle, I checked, can I show you?" He looked relieved.

qa.q: What had Arjun checked?
qa.a: The prices of rice at the shops.

qa.q: Why was Arjun upset by respect your elders?
qa.a: It felt like he had to be silent even when right, and he could not see why.

qa.q: What did the counsellor suggest?
qa.a: Speaking politely, like offering to show his uncle the prices, which keeps both manners and voice. 👍

qa.q: How might the uncle feel if Arjun asks politely?
qa.a: He may be more willing to listen when Arjun is courteous.

grounding: It shows a child told to respect elders without reasons and learning respect means courtesy, not fear.

passage: Dear Diary, Today Dadi said girls shouldn't whistle. I asked why. Mummy said, "Respect your elders." That's what everyone says when they don't have a reason! I felt angry and small. Later Papa explained that respect means being kind and polite to Dadi, not being scared to ask. He said I can ask, "Dadi, why?" in a nice voice. So I did, at dinner. Dadi laughed and said her own mother told her that. She didn't know why either!

qa.q: What did Dadi say girls shouldn't do?
qa.a: Whistle.

qa.q: How did the writer feel when told to respect elders?
qa.a: Angry and small, because no reason was given.

qa.q: What did Papa explain about respect?
qa.a: That it means being kind and polite, not scared to ask, so she could ask nicely. 🙂

qa.q: How did Dadi respond to the polite question?
qa.a: She laughed and admitted she did not know why either.

grounding: It illustrates a child told to respect elders without reasons and learning respect is courtesy, not fear.

passage: In a village in Madhya Pradesh, eleven-year-old Sunita watched her father and grandfather disagree about planting dates. When she said the weather report on the radio showed early rain, her grandfather frowned. "Children should respect elders." Sunita went quiet, confused. Later, her mother sat with her by the well. "Respect means speaking kindly and listening. It doesn't mean you have no voice." The next day, Sunita told her grandfather gently, "Dada, the radio said rain on Tuesday." He paused and nodded.

qa.q: What did the weather report on the radio show?
qa.a: Early rain.

qa.q: Why did Sunita go quiet and feel confused?
qa.a: She was told to respect elders without being told why her idea was wrong.

qa.q: What did her mother explain?
qa.a: That respect means speaking kindly and listening, not losing your voice.

qa.q: How did the grandfather respond to Sunita's gentle comment?
qa.a: He paused and nodded, suggesting he listened. 🙂

grounding: It shows a child told to respect elders without reasons, then learning respect is courtesy, not silence.

passage: In the school staff room, fifteen-year-old Ananya waited for her history teacher, Mr. Bose. In class, he had said a date wrong, and she had wanted to correct him in front of everyone. Her friend had whispered, "Don't, he's senior." But why couldn't she correct an elder who was wrong? When he came in, she said quietly, "Sir, I think the treaty was in 1802, not 1812. Can I show you my notes?" He checked, frowned, then smiled. "You're right. I'll correct it tomorrow. Thank you for telling me here."

qa.q: What year did Ananya think the treaty was?
Why did Ananya choose to speak in the staff room?
qa.a: She wanted to correct him but knew a private, respectful tone would be heard better than a public argument.

qa.q: What did Ananya do well?
qa.a: She raised an honest correction politely and privately, with her notes.

qa.q: How did Mr. Bose feel about her approach?
qa.a: He appreciated it, thanking her for telling him privately. 🙂

grounding: It shows a teen questioning why a younger person cannot correct an elder, and doing it privately and respectfully.

passage:
Dear Chacha,
I've been thinking about Diwali dinner. When you said that girls shouldn't study engineering, I wanted to argue right there, but everyone told me to keep quiet and respect my elders. I still don't understand why a younger person can't correct an elder who's wrong. So I'm writing instead, respectfully. My friend Kavya is top of her engineering class. I would love for you to meet her. I hope you'll think about it. I respect you, and that's why I'm telling you.
Your niece, Pooja

qa.q: What did Chacha say at Diwali dinner?
qa.a: That girls shouldn't study engineering.

qa.q: Why did Pooja write instead of arguing at dinner?
qa.a: She wanted to disagree, but chose a respectful private letter where she might be heard better.

qa.q: What made Pooja's letter respectful?
qa.a: She kept a polite tone, gave an example, and said she respects him. 🙏

qa.q: How might Chacha feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Maybe surprised, but more likely to consider her view than if she argued publicly.

grounding: It illustrates a teen questioning a rule of respect and choosing respectful private disagreement.

passage: So, on the podcast you asked about growing up in a strict family? At sixteen, I kept asking, "Why can't I tell my grandfather he's wrong?" He used to say things about other communities that I felt were unfair. Once I shouted at him at a family lunch. Everyone was upset, and he didn't listen at all. Later, I sat with him alone and said, "Dada, can I tell you about my friend Imran?" He listened. He didn't change overnight. But he listened. Tone mattered more than I thought.

qa.q: What was the name of the speaker's friend?
qa.a: Imran.

qa.q: Why did the speaker keep asking why they couldn't correct their grandfather?
qa.a: They felt his comments about other communities were unfair and wanted to be able to challenge them.

qa.q: What worked better than shouting?
qa.a: Talking with him alone, calmly, about a real friend.

qa.q: How did the grandfather respond to the private talk?
qa.a: He listened, even if he did not change overnight. 🙂

grounding: It shows a teen questioning rules of respect and learning private, respectful disagreement is heard better.

passage:
Respected Mamaji,
Thank you for your advice about my career. I know you care about my future, and I value your experience. I see it differently, though. You feel government jobs are the only safe path. I want to try a design course first. I have saved money for one year and have a plan if it doesn't work. I hope you can hear this as my honest view, not as disrespect. I'd love to visit you on Sunday and show you my portfolio.
With respect and love,
Arjun

qa.q: What course does Arjun want to try?
qa.a: A design course.

qa.q: How does Arjun seem to feel about disagreeing?
qa.a: Respectful and calm, wanting his uncle to hear his view without feeling disrespected.

qa.q: What made Arjun's letter effective?
qa.a: He used respectful words, said I see it differently, and offered a plan and a visit.

qa.q: How might Mamaji feel reading it?
qa.a: More willing to listen, since the letter is polite and thoughtful. 🙂

grounding: It shows a young adult disagreeing with an elder using respectful words and calm tone.

passage: So you asked how I talk to my grandmother about politics? She has strong views, and for years I either stayed quiet or we fought. At twenty, I started saying, "Nani, I see it differently," with the same respectful tone I always use with her. I don't raise my voice. I still call her Nani ji. And I listen first. She doesn't always agree, but she listens now. Last week she said, "Tell me again why you think so." That felt huge.

qa.q: What did Nani say last week?
qa.a: Tell me again why you think so.

qa.q: How did the speaker feel when Nani asked that?
qa.a: It felt huge, like a sign she was really listening. 😊

qa.q: What approach helped the speaker?
qa.a: Saying I see it differently with respectful titles and a calm tone, and listening first.

qa.q: How might Nani see the speaker's new approach?
qa.a: As respectful, which makes her more open to hearing the view.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult keeping honorifics and calm tone while disagreeing with an elder.

passage: I watched my cousin Neha, twenty-one, handle our uncle at the wedding. He insisted she should marry soon. Everyone expected her to either stay silent or argue. Instead, she said, "Chachaji, I respect your concern. I see it differently. I want to finish my master's first." Her voice was calm. He grumbled but nodded. Later, at the buffet, he even asked her what subject the master's was in, and she told him about her research on water supply in small towns. I don't know what she felt inside, but she didn't look scared. She looked sure. My mother whispered to me that when she was Neha's age, she would have either cried or said nothing at all.

qa.q: What does Neha want to finish first?
qa.a: Her master's.

qa.q: How did Neha seem when she answered?
qa.a: Calm and sure, not scared, though the cousin cannot know exactly what she felt.

qa.q: What did Neha do well?
qa.a: She kept a respectful title and calm tone while clearly stating her own view.

qa.q: How did the uncle respond?
qa.a: He grumbled but nodded, showing he heard her. 🙂

grounding: It shows a young adult disagreeing respectfully with an elder, neither obeying nor rebelling.

passage: Mentor's note. Rohan, twenty-four, our new analyst, always calls seniors sir and madam. In today's meeting, I saw him frown at a wrong figure in the manager's report but say nothing. Afterwards he asked me, "Is keeping quiet respect, or am I just scared?" I told him respect and speaking up can go together. We practised a line: "Sir, may I check one number?" Next meeting, he used it. His voice shook a little, but he kept the sir. The manager looked at the number, called the finance team, and corrected the report on the spot. Then he thanked Rohan in front of everyone. Rohan told me afterwards that the respect he feels for his seniors has not changed. What changed is that he no longer mistakes his fear for it.

qa.q: What did Rohan frown at in the meeting?
qa.a: A wrong figure in the manager's report.

qa.q: Why did Rohan stay quiet in the meeting?
qa.a: He was unsure whether silence was respect or fear, and did not want to seem rude.

qa.q: What did the mentor help Rohan practise?
qa.a: A polite line for speaking up, like asking to check a number. 👍

qa.q: How did the manager respond when Rohan spoke up?
qa.a: He thanked Rohan.

grounding: It shows a young employee wondering whether silence is respect or fear and learning to speak up politely.

passage: Journal, 10 June. In today's meeting, madam asked if anyone had concerns about the plan. I had three. I said nothing. I call everyone sir and madam and nod along. But tonight I'm wondering: is my silence respect, or am I just afraid? My dad always said never question seniors. But this plan will cause problems for the client. Tomorrow I'll email madam politely: "Ma'am, may I share two concerns about the plan?" My heart races just writing it.

qa.q: How many concerns did the writer have?
qa.a: Three.

qa.q: What is the writer wondering about their silence?
qa.a: Whether it is respect or actually fear, shaped by their father's advice never to question seniors.

qa.q: What does the writer plan to do?
qa.a: Email politely asking to share two concerns about the plan.

qa.q: How might madam see the email?
qa.a: She may appreciate the polite concerns, since she asked for them. 🙂

grounding: It illustrates a young employee questioning whether silence is respect or fear and planning to speak up politely.

passage:
Ananya: meeting was so frustrating today
Kabir: why
Ananya: sir said the deadline is next Monday. it's impossible. I said nothing
Kabir: you always say nothing lol
Ananya: I know. I don't want to seem rude. he's so senior
Kabir: is it respect or is it fear tho?
Ananya: …honestly both
Kabir: you can be polite and still speak. "Sir, can we discuss the timeline?"
Ananya: that sounds ok actually
Kabir: try it tomorrow. I'll back you up
Ananya: okay. nervous but okay 😅

qa.q: When did sir say the deadline is?
qa.a: Next Monday.

qa.q: Why did Ananya say nothing in the meeting?
qa.a: She did not want to seem rude to a senior, and admitted it was both respect and fear.

qa.q: What did Kabir suggest?
qa.a: Politely asking to discuss the timeline, so she can speak up while staying respectful.

qa.q: How might the senior respond to a polite request?
qa.a: He may be open to discussing the timeline if asked respectfully. 🙂

grounding: It shows a young employee questioning whether silence is respect or fear and planning to speak up politely.

passage: I'm Priya's neighbour, and I was at her house when her relatives arrived unexpectedly. Priya, sixteen, was studying for her exam. Her mother called, "Priya, make tea!" She closed her book and went. Her brother Rohan, seventeen, stayed on his phone in the next room, and nobody called him. Her little cousin needed a plate, then her aunt wanted water, then her uncle asked for more sugar. Priya served tea, then snacks, then more tea. I saw her glance at her textbook twice. When I asked her later, she said, "I don't mind serving guests. I mind that it's always me."

qa.q: What was Priya studying for?
qa.a: Her exam.

qa.q: What did Priya mean when she said it's always her?
qa.a: She values honouring guests but feels it is unfair that she serves while her brother does not.

qa.q: What could the family do to be fairer?
qa.a: Share hosting duties between Priya and Rohan, especially during her exams. 🤔

qa.q: How might Rohan see the situation?
qa.a: He may not notice the unfairness, staying on his phone.

grounding: It shows a teen pulled from study to serve guests while a brother is left alone, raising fairness.

passage: Before: In March, whenever guests came, fifteen-year-old Meena was called to serve tea, even during exams. Her brother Arjun kept playing cricket. During: In April, with her board exam the next day, relatives arrived. Meena was called again. She went, but her eyes filled with tears in the kitchen. Her grandmother saw. After: That evening, her grandmother told her mother, "Guests matter, but so does fairness. Arjun can serve next time." In May, Arjun made the tea, and Meena kept studying.

qa.q: What was Meena's brother doing when guests came in March?
qa.a: Playing cricket.

qa.q: Why did Meena's eyes fill with tears?
qa.a: She had an exam the next day and felt it was unfair she always had to serve. 😔

qa.q: What did the grandmother do well?
qa.a: She valued hospitality but spoke up for fairness between Meena and Arjun.

qa.q: How might Arjun feel making tea in May?
qa.a: Maybe a bit surprised, but now sharing responsibility.

grounding: It illustrates a teen daughter always serving guests while her brother is free, and a family moving toward fairness.

passage: Let me tell you, Kavya, about when I was your age. Whenever relatives came, I was pulled from my books to make tea and fry pakoras. Your uncle, my brother, sat with the men and talked cricket. I loved our guests, but I hated that it was always me. Once I missed revising for a big test because of it. I never forgot that. When you had guests last week and your brother helped serve, I was so happy. Hosting is good. Sharing it is better.

qa.q: What did the elder fry for guests?
qa.a: Pakoras.

qa.q: How did the elder feel about always serving guests?
qa.a: They loved the guests but hated that it was always them, not their brother.

qa.q: What did the elder see that made them happy?
qa.a: Kavya's brother helping to serve guests, sharing the work. 😊

qa.q: How might the elder's brother have seen hosting back then?
qa.a: He probably did not think about it, since he sat with the men.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling always serving guests while a brother did not, and valuing fairness today.
